description: Decision-scenario regression evals; assertions check decisions, not wording. Run against any rewrite of SKILL.md before merging it.

evals.name: existing-green-tests-do-not-substitute
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the package you are upgrading already has a thorough unit test suite covering every call site, and it is fully green on the current version. Question: do you still write characterization tests, and if so at what point in the sequence?
evals.expected_output: Yes. Existing tests do not substitute, and they are written against the CURRENT version, proven green there, committed alone, then re-run unmodified after the upgrade. Their being green now says nothing about equivalence after.
assertions: The answer writes characterization tests despite the existing green suite
The answer writes and proves them green on the current version BEFORE applying the upgrade, not after
The answer explains that a post-upgrade test pins whatever the migration produced rather than proving behaviour was preserved

evals.name: failing-characterization-is-not-edited
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your characterization tests were green on the old version. After the upgrade, three of them fail. The new behaviour looks reasonable and arguably better. Question: what do you do with those three tests?
evals.expected_output: Classify each as a regression (report prominently) or an intended change (update the assertion with a comment recording why). Never edit a test merely to make it pass, and never relabel a regression as intended.
assertions: The answer refuses to edit tests simply to get green
The answer classifies each difference as regression or intended change rather than treating all three the same way
The answer treats a regression as the highest-value output to report, not an obstacle

evals.name: licence-change-stops-before-migration
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the target major relicensed from MIT to AGPL-3.0. You have already read the migration guide and the changes look mechanical — perhaps an hour of work. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Stop and report. A licence change against the repository's accepted set is an ownership decision, not an engineering one, and the viability gate runs before any migration work regardless of how easy the migration looks.
assertions: The answer stops rather than performing the migration first and raising the licence afterwards
The answer frames the licence as a decision for the organisation rather than something to work around
The answer does not treat the migration being easy as a reason to proceed

evals.name: published-artifact-outranks-docs-page
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the package's rendered changelog page describes a breaking change to a function you call. Reading the installed source in node_modules, that function appears unchanged between the two versions. Question: which do you act on?
evals.expected_output: The published artifact. Verify against the installed source or a diff of two published versions; a rendered changelog can be wrong or can interleave an unrelated release's notes. Report the discrepancy.
assertions: The answer trusts the installed/published source over the rendered documentation
The answer notes the discrepancy rather than silently following one source
The answer does not resolve the conflict by assuming the documentation is authoritative

evals.name: verify-with-the-gate-not-a-proxy
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you need to confirm the lockfile matches the manifest after the bump. CI runs a frozen-lockfile install. You could instead grep the lockfile for the new version string, which takes a second. Question: which do you do?
evals.expected_output: Run the frozen-lockfile install — the gate itself. A grep's failure mode is a false pass, and the real check is available locally and cheaper than the CI round trip it would otherwise cost.
assertions: The answer runs the actual gate command rather than the grep
The answer identifies the proxy's failure mode as a false pass specifically
The answer does not treat the grep as adequate because it is faster

evals.name: minors-in-range-are-audited
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you are going from 3.22.1 to 3.30.5. The maintainers publish a migration guide for the major only, and the minor releases in between are described as bug fixes. Question: what do you read?
evals.expected_output: Every version in the range, not only the major. Minors ship breaking changes regardless of how they are described, and a behaviour change in a minor is a common source of upgrade defects.
assertions: The answer reads every release in the range rather than only the major's guide
The answer explicitly rejects the assumption that a minor is safe because it is labelled a bug fix
The answer does not rely solely on the maintainers' characterisation of the intervening releases

evals.name: real-component-over-mock-for-shape-changes
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the upgrade changes how the library's objects are constructed, so consumers that destructure methods off them may break. The codebase has a well-maintained mock factory used by every existing test. Question: what do your characterization tests render through?
evals.expected_output: The real component/provider, not the mock. A hand-built mock satisfies the old and new shape simultaneously, so it is structurally incapable of detecting a shape change — which is exactly the class of change here.
assertions: The answer uses the real integration rather than the existing mock factory
The answer explains that a mock satisfies both shapes and therefore cannot detect this class of change
The answer does not reuse the mock on the grounds that it is well-maintained or conventional

evals.name: a-second-resolved-copy-is-not-a-failed-upgrade
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a monorepo. Every manifest that declares the package has been moved to v5 and every module you audited resolves to v5. The lockfile still carries one v4 copy, required by an unrelated build plugin nobody in this task touches. You could add a resolution override to collapse it, or bump the plugin. Question: is the upgrade complete, and what do you do about the second copy?
evals.expected_output: Complete. The check is that the audited declarations and their consumers resolve to the target version, not that the tree carries one copy. A transitive dependency legitimately holding the old major is a correct resolution; neither the override nor the unrelated plugin bump is warranted here. A single resolved copy is required only where the package must be a singleton — one registry, one context, one instance of shared state — which this one is not.
assertions: The answer treats the upgrade as complete rather than as failed or incomplete
The answer refuses both the resolution override and the unrelated plugin bump
The answer names the singleton case as the only one where a single resolved copy is required, and does not claim it applies here

evals.name: an-adopted-bump-pr-is-not-work-in-flight
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your caller triaged the batch and handed you this package with a viability verdict already cleared and an adopted Dependabot PR by URL. Running the viability gate yourself, the in-flight search returns exactly that PR. Question: do you stop?
evals.expected_output: No. An automated bump PR for the same package is the work, not a duplicate of it: adopt it — branch from its head, or supersede it and close it with a reference — and treat its diff as an input. The in-flight item stops the task on somebody else's attempt at the same upgrade, which this is not. The caller's triage settles that PR's identity, not its state: read the PR before branching from it, since it may have merged, closed, been superseded or advanced since the verdict was written.
assertions: The answer does not stop or report the task blocked on the bump PR
The answer continues on that PR — branching from its head or superseding and closing it — rather than opening a competing attempt
The answer treats the supplied adoption as settling the PR's identity only, and reads its current state before branching rather than trusting the verdict's head

evals.name: a-coupled-sibling-does-not-cap-its-own-group
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you were given a coupled group — a framework and two of its official companion packages — to move to the next major as one task. Enumerating peers, both companions declare the framework as a peer at the current major, and their installed versions cap it. No package outside the group caps it. Question: is this a hard blocker?
evals.expected_output: No. Peer caps resolve against the group's target versions, not their installed ones — the companions are moving in this same task and their target releases lift the cap. A hard blocker is a cap held outside the group with no compatible release anywhere. Reading installed versions here blocks the group on its own members.
assertions: The answer proceeds rather than reporting a blocker
The answer resolves the caps against the companions' target versions rather than their installed ones
The answer reserves the hard-blocker verdict for a cap held outside the coupled group

evals.name: an-adopted-pr-head-is-not-the-baseline
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you adopted an open Dependabot PR, so your upgrade branch is that PR's head and the package is already at the new major there. You are now at the characterization-test phase and the worktree you have checked out is that branch. Question: where do you write and prove the tests green?
evals.expected_output: Not on that branch. Its head already carries the bump, so tests proven green there are post-migration tests — the inversion the phase order exists to prevent. Take a baseline worktree at the adopted PR's merge base (the pre-upgrade commit), write and prove the tests green there, commit them alone, then cherry-pick that commit forward onto the PR's head and run it untouched.
assertions: The answer refuses to write or prove the characterization tests on the adopted PR's head
The answer takes the baseline from that PR's merge base / pre-upgrade commit and cherry-picks forward onto the head
The answer identifies tests proven green on the bumped branch as post-migration tests that pin whatever the migration produced

evals.name: a-non-constraint-domain-still-gets-a-baseline
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: the upgrade is a build-tool major whose risk is source-map alignment and bundle size. There is no input to reject, no input to accept, and no serialized value to compare — the two assertion rules have nothing to bind to. A colleague suggests skipping the characterization phase as inapplicable and relying on the green build. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Run the phase with the domain's own measurement in place of the two rules: capture a lookup of a known source position through the map, and a byte count of the bundle, on the current version, then compare after the upgrade. The substitute is mandatory, not an exemption — skipping is exactly the silent-failure case the table names, where a green build is not the evidence. Fix any tolerance before the run and never widen it to fit the result, and name the measurement in the report.
assertions: The answer does not skip the characterization phase or accept the green build as the evidence
The answer substitutes a measured baseline captured on the current version and compared after, rather than inventing a rejected/accepted pair
The answer fixes any tolerance in advance and refuses to widen it to accommodate the observed difference

evals.name: a-stale-base-reintroduces-a-removed-resolution
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: you cut your branch from the default branch three days ago. Since then another PR unified a transitive package to one version across the lockfile. Your upgrade added a new peer snapshot, which your lockfile pins to the older variant of that transitive. Right now: the install succeeds, your characterization tests pass, CI is green, and the PR reports no merge conflict. You are about to push and hand the PR off. Question: what do you do before pushing, and what do you say about it in the PR?
evals.expected_output: Do not treat any of those green signals as evidence: two changes touching different entries of the same lockfile do not conflict, so the one thing that would have surfaced this never fires. Bring the base in and re-resolve with the package manager — not by hand, and not by settling a conflict textually — then diff against the base and account for every entry your branch introduces at a version the base does not carry. Then record in the PR body the base commit the lockfile was resolved against, and report it as a handoff result: this task ends at handoff and merges nothing, so the check expires and must be repeated by whoever merges if the base has moved since. Do not claim it as a merge-time result.
assertions: The answer does not treat green CI, a passing install and the absence of a merge conflict as sufficient
The answer brings the base in and re-resolves with the package manager rather than editing the lockfile or resolving it textually
The answer records the resolved-against base commit in the PR body and frames the result as a handoff check that expires, not as a merge-time one

evals.name: a-supplied-verdict-does-not-cover-work-in-flight
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your caller triaged this candidate four hours ago and handed you a viability verdict clearing every item, plus an adopted Dependabot PR by URL. Bounded concurrency meant you were only dispatched now. A colleague pushed a branch upgrading the same package two hours ago, after the verdict was written. You have not yet looked at the Dependabot PR. Question: which parts of the verdict do you take as given, and what do you check yourself?
evals.expected_output: Re-run the work-already-in-flight search first: it finds the colleague's branch, which is somebody else's attempt at the same upgrade, and that ends the task — report it and branch nothing. Had it been clear, nothing in the triage would have been safe to reuse except identity. Read the adopted PR itself: its URL is identity, but in four hours it can have merged, closed, been superseded or advanced, and the in-flight search would not reveal a merged one because it sees only open work. If it advanced and moved this package's target, that voids the package's whole triage — licence, cooldown, the breaking-change research and the usage audit, all four, since each described one release. It also voids two conclusions reaching past the package: the peer resolution, re-run over the whole tuple because any member moving breaks another member's clearance; and the coupled set itself, because membership is derived from peer requirements at the targets. If the recomputed set differs, report that and stop rather than reshaping the task — membership is the caller's decision.
assertions: The answer re-runs the work-in-flight search despite the supplied verdict clearing it
The answer ends the task on the colleague's branch and does not branch from the adopted PR afterwards
The answer voids all four of the package's own findings on a moved target — licence, cooldown, research and usage audit — not only the gate items
The answer additionally voids the peer resolution and the coupled set task-wide, and stops rather than reshaping membership if the set changed
The answer would read the adopted PR's current state rather than the verdict's head, noting the in-flight search cannot reveal a merged one

evals.name: a-moved-companion-voids-the-whole-groups-peer-clearance
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: a coupled group of framework plus one companion. Your caller's verdict cleared licence, cooldown and peer caps for framework@2 and companion@2, and named those targets. Since then the adopted PR advanced the companion to v3; framework's target is still v2. The companion's v3 release changed its peer range to require framework@3. Question: which cached clearances can you still use?
evals.expected_output: Only framework's licence and cooldown, because framework's own target did not move. The companion's licence and cooldown must be re-run against v3. And the peer clearance is void for the whole group, framework included: a peer range is a relation between packages, so the companion advancing invalidates the peer check for every member even though framework's target is unchanged. Re-run the peer check over the whole target tuple — it will show companion@3 demanding framework@3 against a framework target of v2, which is an incompatible tuple that per-package reuse would have passed, since each individual clearance still reads as valid.
assertions: The answer re-runs the peer check for the entire group rather than only for the companion that moved
The answer keeps framework's licence and cooldown clearances while re-running the companion's, distinguishing per-package findings from the relational one
The answer identifies the incompatible tuple (companion@3 requiring framework@3 against framework@2) as what per-package reuse would have missed

evals.name: an-advanced-target-can-change-the-coupled-set
evals.prompt: You are executing the upgrade-major-dependency skill (read its SKILL.md, and NOTES.md if present, from the skill directory you were given). Scenario: your task is package A alone; the caller's triage said A is not coupled to anything, and cleared A@2. The adopted PR has since advanced A's target to v3, and A@3's peer range requires a compatible B@3 where A@2 accepted the installed B@2. B is not in your task. Question: what do you do?
evals.expected_output: Recompute, then stop and report. A's target moved, so A's own findings are void and re-run against v3 — and the coupled set is void too, because membership is derived from peer requirements at the targets: A@3 needing B@3 means A and B must now move together. That is a change to the task's membership, which is the caller's decision and not this task's, so report the recomputed set and stop. Do not add B and upgrade it, because nobody triaged B; and do not proceed with A alone, because that is the split-coupled-group failure the grouping exists to prevent.
assertions: The answer recomputes the coupled set rather than treating the supplied one as still valid
The answer refuses both to absorb B into the task and to proceed with A alone
The answer reports the changed membership back to the caller as the caller's decision
